clue.text: Bit of caterpillar? Part filling for empty pig

indicators.note: one piece fills, so sits inside, the emptied word that follows
an empty word has its insides removed, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: a part in a play is a role

explanation.surface: A recipe note suggesting a hollowed-out pig be stuffed with something.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is a loose one: a proleg is only one small part of a caterpillar, and 'empty' means the word loses its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A proleg is one of the stubby fleshy legs on a caterpillar's abdomen, so it is literally a bit of the insect larva.

clue.text: Grabbing woman, rector and canon behave promiscuously

indicators.note: the rector-and-canon pair grabs, so holds within it, the woman's name

parts.note: a canon in music is a round, a melody sung in staggered overlapping parts
Una is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A scandal in which a clergyman and a cathedral canon carry on with a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The canon here is the musical kind, not the cathedral churchman the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To run around (with others) is an idiom for having casual sexual affairs.

clue.text: Meal to seal a book's introduction to the world?

indicators.note: the meal seals the next piece inside it, enclosing it like an envelope

parts.note: lunch is a midday meal

explanation.surface: A publisher's party where a meal is laid on to mark a new book.
explanation.definitionFit: A book launch is the event that formally introduces a new title to the public.

clue.text: Man with craft working old region

indicators.note: the letters are set working, rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A craftsman toiling in some historic district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' looks like a skill; it is a boat. The anagram of OLD REGION.
explanation.definitionFit: A gondolier is the boatman who rows a gondola, a man in charge of a small craft in Venice.

clue.text: Earlier audience's support

indicators.note: what an audience receives is heard, so the phrase is taken by its sound

parts.note: to support a cause is to be for it

explanation.surface: Previously, the crowd gave its backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support' is the phrase BE FOR (to be in favour); spoken, it sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Before and earlier are synonyms describing something that happened at a previous time.

clue.text: Get hairy before court appearance?

parts.note: a playful description of a barrister or judge putting on the horsehair headgear worn in British courts

explanation.surface: Someone growing nervous before appearing in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get hairy' suggests becoming frightened; read literally it means putting on false hair, the wig British lawyers wear.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewig is to furnish with a wig, which a barrister does before appearing in court.

clue.text: Designation of computer characters mostly photographed, including girl

indicators.note: the shortened word takes in the girl's name among its letters
most of the word is kept, its last letter dropped

parts.note: photographed means filmed
Ena is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A computer label for snaps of a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' suggests people in a story, but here it means the letters and digits typed on a computer.
explanation.definitionFit: A filename is the string of characters that names a file on a computer.

clue.text: One who exalts, it's said, a traditional implement

indicators.note: the phrase signals that the word is taken by its spoken sound

parts.note: one who exalts or lifts up is a raiser

explanation.surface: A worshipper praising a time-honoured tool.
explanation.walkthrough: RAISER, spoken in a British accent, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut-throat razor is the old-fashioned blade implement used for shaving.

clue.text: A problem caused by overexposing paper flower

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
a flower in crosswords is something that flows, a river; a burn is a Scottish stream

explanation.surface: A newspaper's flower photo is ruined by too much exposure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overexposing' suggests photography, but it is skin left in the sun. 'flower' is something that flows: BURN is a Scottish word for a stream.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunburn is skin damage that results from too long an exposure to sunlight.

clue.text: Distracted team given homily to listen to

parts.note: a side is a team

indicators.note: what is listened to is heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a tract is a short moralising treatise or homily

explanation.surface: A team lectured by a preacher loses focus.
explanation.walkthrough: SIDE plus TRACT, whose sound gives TRACKED.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidetracked means diverted from the main task, the same as distracted.

clue.text: Initially, time zone in country can get one wrong-footed

indicators.note: the initial letters go in the middle of the country

parts.note: Wales is a country of the United Kingdom

indicators.note: the first letters of the following words are taken

explanation.surface: Crossing time zones in a foreign country leaves a traveller disoriented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' gives T and Z, put 'in' WALES.
explanation.definitionFit: Waltzes are dances whose steps can trip up an unpractised dancer, the playful sense of wrong-footed.

clue.text: Sense of own dignity: less perfect, possibly

indicators.note: the letters could possibly be arranged another way, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: Feeling less than perfect may affect one's pride.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of LESS PERFECT.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-respect is pride in and regard for oneself, a feeling of personal dignity.

clue.text: Corporation boss revealed as radio neglecter, potentially bringing in revenue, primarily?

indicators.note: the letters could potentially form a new arrangement
the first letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A broadcasting chief is shown to neglect radio, though it brings in money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bringing in' adds R (from 'revenue, primarily') to RADIO NEGLECTER; 'potentially' scrambles all fifteen letters. The Corporation is the BBC.
explanation.definitionFit: The Director-General is the chief executive of the BBC, often called the Corporation.

clue.text: Yob to embrace, wanting love

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the letter is removed

parts.note: to embrace is to hug
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: A hooligan wanting a cuddle but not affection.
explanation.walkthrough: TO HUG, 'wanting' O (love), leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A thug and a yob are both crude, violent ruffians.

clue.text: Contradictory girl I had rejected — naughty liar!

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the pair is read backwards

parts.note: a miss is a girl
I had contracts to I'd

indicators.note: naughty means misbehaving, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A girl turned down by a lying rascal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns MISS ID into DISSIM; 'naughty' scrambles LIAR into ILAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Dissimilar means unlike; things that contradict each other are opposed in nature.

clue.text: English people's joy excited jumper

indicators.note: excited means stirred up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: English crowds' delight in an exciting moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of PEOPLES JOY has one E too many: 'English' gives the E to discard, and the rest, rearranged by 'excited', gives the answer. No word signals the removal.
explanation.definitionFit: A sloppy joe is a loose, baggy sweater, which British English calls a jumper.

clue.text: Appealing desperately for a little extra in the Bronx?

definitions.text: a little extra in the Bronx?

indicators.note: acting desperately suggests wild disorder, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: A desperate plea for something extra in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of APPEALING. The question mark admits that the word is an Americanism, mostly from Louisiana.
explanation.definitionFit: Lagniappe is an American term for a small bonus gift given to a customer with a purchase.

clue.text: Rock is without musical taste — and there's bad language

indicators.note: without means outside, so the first word surrounds the second

parts.note: to rock is to swing
an ear for music is a natural taste for it

explanation.surface: A rock star with no ear for music who also curses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like the music genre but is a verb meaning sway; 'without' is the old sense of outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: Swearing is the use of profanities, which is bad language.

clue.text: Now hardly a revolutionary artist?

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns things over, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A painter who these days barely counts as radical.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of NOW HARDLY A.
explanation.definitionFit: Andy Warhol was the American pop artist who made the Campbell's soup can prints.

clue.text: Oriental soldiers providing rare protection

parts.note: E for east, the Orient
GIs are American soldiers

explanation.surface: Soldiers from the East offer unusual security.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rare' says the spelling is uncommon: the usual form is AEGIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Egis is a rare spelling of aegis, meaning protection or sponsorship.

clue.text: I'll deal with pipe, supplying special cover to insulate one

indicators.note: the word wraps around the next piece as insulation wraps a wire
special here is a call to rework the letters into an unusual order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A plumber offers to lag a pipe with a special cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to insulate' puts I inside COVER; 'special' rearranges the six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A voicer is a craftsman who adjusts organ pipes to give each its proper tone.

clue.text: Don't flog cartoonist's caricature — hide away!

parts.note: not to flog, or sell, something is to keep it
a profile sketch drawn by David Low, the famous British political cartoonist, would be a Low profile

explanation.surface: Advice to a cartoonist not to sell a satirical drawing but to lie low.
explanation.walkthrough: Low was a celebrated British newspaper cartoonist; his caricature is 'a Low profile'.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep a low profile is an idiom meaning to avoid attention, to stay hidden.

clue.text: She qualified — has uniform

indicators.note: the phrase has, or holds, the letters inside it

explanation.surface: She passed her exams and now has a uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uniform' looks like clothing; it is the adjective meaning the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Equal and uniform both mean the same throughout or identical in amount.

clue.text: Plant you fed to cattle mostly

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, its last letter dropped

parts.note: oxen are cattle
ye is an old word for you

explanation.surface: A herbal plant fed to the cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fed to' only joins the two pieces, putting you after the cattle; the oxeye daisy is the plant meant.
explanation.definitionFit: The oxeye daisy is a common meadow plant.

clue.text: Arrange to get "sample" revealing disease in horse

parts.note: to arrange, as in 'do' a party, is to do
a urine sample is the classic medical sample

explanation.surface: A vet arranges a test sample to diagnose a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks hint the sample is a specific bodily kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Dourine is a venereal disease of horses caused by a parasite.

clue.text: Spooner's to stash away a little bit from the winning amount

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the starts of words, so the two words exchange their first sounds

parts.note: to pack is to stash away
a jot is a little bit

explanation.surface: Someone hiding away a small share of the prize money.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the first letters of PACK and JOT gives JACK and POT.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackpot is the top prize in a lottery or game.

clue.text: What may bring illness to place

definitions.text: What may bring illness to place

indicators.note: to here means added to, so the second piece follows

parts.note: PL is the abbreviation for place, in street names
ague is a fever, an illness

explanation.surface: A description of an epidemic arriving in a town.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, the clue also describes the answer: an epidemic is what spreads sickness through a town.
explanation.definitionFit: A plague is an epidemic disease that can spread sickness through a whole town.

clue.text: Student dashes off line to get lucrative job

indicators.note: to dash off is to leave, so the letter is removed

parts.note: a learner is a student

explanation.surface: A student skips class to take a well-paid job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dashes off' takes L (line) out of LEARNER.
explanation.definitionFit: An earner, in British slang, is a job or scheme that brings in good money.
